name: Lozi Kingdom (Barotseland)
summary: The kingdom of the Lozi people on the upper Zambezi floodplain, led by the Litunga; the Kololo ruled it 1840–64. A British protectorate from 1890, it became part of Zambia in 1964.

knownFor.label: Kuomboka
knownFor.note: Royal move to high ground in the floods.

knownFor.label: Nalikwanda barge
knownFor.note: Royal barge with a giant elephant.

terrain.value: The broad grassy Bulozi (Barotse) floodplain of the upper Zambezi, flooded every year, with raised mounds for villages, ringed by dry woodland on Kalahari sands.

climate.value: Tropical, with a hot rainy season from about November to April; the flood peaks around March–April, when the Litunga moves to higher ground in the Kuomboka ceremony.

resources.value: Fish, cattle, grain from the floodplain.

disasters.value: Unusually high or low floods could ruin crops; droughts, cattle disease (rinderpest swept the region in the 1890s) and famine.

population.value: Perhaps 100,000–200,000 people in the 1800s, including the Lozi (Luyi) and many subject peoples.

urbanisation.value: Mostly villages; a royal capital and market towns.

disease.value: Malaria and other tropical diseases; smallpox outbreaks.

migration.value: The Kololo, a Sotho group led by Sebitwane, moved north and conquered the floodplain about 1840; Lozi royals fled north until 1864.

economicBase.value: Farming of sorghum, millet, maize and later cassava on floodplain mounds and gardens, large cattle herds grazed on the plain, and fishing.

tradeRoutes.value: Ivory, cattle and captives were traded with Ovimbundu (Mambari) caravans from Angola; traders from the south, such as George Westbeech, came from the 1870s.

wealth.value: Wealth lay in cattle, ivory and tribute; the Litunga redistributed food and goods paid by subject peoples.

moneyAndTax.value: Tribute, market taxes and trade goods; cowrie shells in many markets.

inequality.value: Rulers and nobles above free farmers; enslaved people at the bottom.

governmentType.value: A monarchy under the Litunga, advised by the Kuta (council of indunas, or officials), with a southern capital at Nalolo ruled by a royal princess.

keyRulers.value: Mboo, the first Litunga in tradition; Mulambwa (early 1800s); Lewanika (1878–1916, briefly overthrown 1884–85), who signed treaties with the British.

succession.value: The Litunga was chosen by the Kuta from male descendants of earlier kings, so rival princes often competed for the throne.

institutions.value: The Kuta council of indunas, headed by the Ngambela (chief minister), and makolo units that organised labour and military service.

stability.value: The Kololo ruled the floodplain about 1840–64; after their fall, coups and civil wars troubled the 1870s and 1880s.

eliteConflict.value: Rival princes and indunas fought over the throne; Lewanika was overthrown in a rebellion in 1884 before regaining power in 1885.

armyAndTech.value: Armies of spearmen raised through the makolo system, large canoe fleets on the floodplain, and guns obtained through trade in the 1800s.

majorWars.value: The Lozi uprising of 1864 under Sipopa overthrew the Kololo rulers; raids on neighbouring peoples followed.

territoryChange.value: Lozi power spread from the floodplain over neighbouring peoples in the 1700s–1800s; a 1905 border award gave part of the west to Portuguese Angola.

alliancesRivals.value: Treaty with the British South Africa Company (1890).

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded; the Lozi built mounds, canals and drainage works to farm the floodplain.

scienceEducation.value: Oral learning; Qur’anic schools where Islam spread.

openness.value: Open to traders and missionaries, especially under Lewanika, who welcomed the Paris Evangelical Mission and sought British protection.

communicationTransport.value: Dugout canoes and barges on the Zambezi and floodplain channels, footpaths through the woodland, and messengers carrying royal orders.

languageWriting.value: Silozi, a language close to Sesotho that grew out of the Kololo period; the older Luyana language survived at court and in rituals.

artsArchitecture.value: Fine basketry and wood carving, the royal barge Nalikwanda, and the Kuomboka ceremony, when the court moves to higher ground.

socialStructure.value: The Litunga and royal family, indunas (officials), commoner Lozi, subject peoples who paid tribute, and enslaved or serf labourers.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the Litunga and the floodplain; the Silozi language and the Kuomboka gave many peoples a shared Lozi identity.

dailyLife.value: Villages stood on mounds above the flood; families farmed, herded cattle and fished, and moved to the edge of the plain when the waters rose.

neighbours.value: The Tonga, Luvale, Lunda and Mbunda peoples, Ndebele raiders from the south-east, and later Portuguese Angola and the British South Africa Company.

ideasReligions.value: Sacred kingship: the Litunga was linked to royal ancestors whose graves were shrines; Christianity spread through missions from the 1880s.

colonisation.value: Lewanika signed the Lochner Concession with the British South Africa Company (1890); Barotseland became a protectorate within British Central Africa.

riseSignals.value: According to oral tradition, the Luyi (Lozi) kingdom formed on the floodplain in the 1600s under kings descended from Mboo.

peakPeriod.value: Under Lewanika (1878–1916), who ruled much of today’s western Zambia and kept a special status under British rule.

declineSignals.value: Barotseland was absorbed into Northern Rhodesia in 1911, and the Litunga’s powers were reduced step by step.

outcome.value: Part of Zambia (1964); the Litunga remains.

overallCertainty.value: Known from oral traditions, travellers and colonial records; many dates are approximate.
